response.response_text:
## Two Peoples, One Whakapapa (Genealogy)

Cook Island Māori and New Zealand Māori are distinct peoples with separate cultural identities, languages, and histories — yet they share deep ancestral roots that connect them across the Pacific.

## Origins and Shared Ancestry

The two groups are closely related by whakapapa. It is likely that some ancestors of New Zealand Māori arrived from the Cook Islands around 700 years ago. [[1]](cite://1/1) Oral traditions from Aitutaki in the Cook Islands even claim that the famous Tainui waka (canoe) stopped there on its voyage from Ra'iatea to New Zealand, and Cook Islanders rekindled links with the Tainui iwi (tribe) in the 1990s. [[2]](cite://2/1) The two peoples share place names, and even family names — for example, Paikea, which originated with a family from Mauke who settled near East Cape in New Zealand. [[2]](cite://2/2)

There is, however, a touch of friendly sibling rivalry in this relationship. As one journalist has noted, "there is a bit of stick between Cook Islands Maori and New Zealand Maori. One group maintains they kicked the other out a thousand years ago … The voyagers claim those who stayed behind were the slack ones!" [[1]](cite://1/2)

## Different Homelands, Different Status

A key distinction is that New Zealand Māori are the *tangata whenua* — the people of the land — and are recognised as the original inhabitants of Aotearoa New Zealand. [[3]](cite://3/1) Their history in New Zealand includes a rich oral culture, centuries of settlement, the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, land wars, and a long struggle for cultural and political recognition. [[4]](cite://4/1)

Cook Island Māori, by contrast, are a Pacific community who originate from the Cook Islands — a self-governing nation in free association with New Zealand. Cook Islanders hold New Zealand citizenship but come from a separate homeland with its own governance. [[5]](cite://5/1)

## Language: Related but Distinct

Both peoples speak Māori languages that fall under the same Tahitic branch of the Austronesian language family, which means the dialects of the Cook Islands are *very* similar to te reo Māori. [[2]](cite://2/3)[[6]](cite://6/1) However, they are separate languages. Cook Islands Māori (te reo Māori Kūki 'Airani) has several island dialects, with Rarotongan emerging as the dominant form. [[7]](cite://7/1)

Sadly, both languages face pressure. Among Cook Islanders living in New Zealand, only 18% could hold an everyday conversation in Cook Islands Māori by 2001, and by 2018 that figure had dropped further to just 10%. [[8]](cite://8/1) Language nests (*punanga reo*) and school programmes have been introduced to help revive it. [[8]](cite://8/2) UNESCO lists te reo Māori Kūki 'Airani as one of the most endangered Pacific languages. [[9]](cite://9/1)

## Culture and Community

While New Zealand Māori culture is organised around iwi (tribes) and hapū (sub-tribes) with a strong focus on land, Cook Island Māori culture centres on the *kopu tangata* — the extended family — as a powerful unifying force. [[10]](cite://10/1) Cook Island cultural traditions such as embroidering *tīvaevae* (colourful quilts), the ritual of cutting a boy's hair at adolescence, and energetic dance and drumming performances remain important expressions of identity. [[10]](cite://10/2)

Today, Cook Island Māori are the third largest Pacific community in Aotearoa New Zealand [[9]](cite://9/2), and around 90,000 people identify as both Māori and Pacific — a reflection of just how intertwined these communities have become. [[11]](cite://11/1)

---

1.document_title: Cook Islanders: Migration, Settlement, and Cultural Identity in New Zealand
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the migration history and settlement patterns of Cook Islanders in New Zealand from the early 20th century through 2018. Beginning with small numbers of soldiers and students in the 1920s-1930s, migration accelerated significantly after WWII as young people sought better wages and urban opportunities. By 1976, over 12,000 Cook Islanders had settled in New Zealand, eventually reaching 61,000 by 2013 and over 80,000 by 2018—outnumbering those remaining on the islands. Early migrants concentrated in major cities including Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch, working in factory, domestic, canning, and timber mill jobs. Chain migration became prevalent from the 1960s onward as established residents sponsored family members. Economic factors, including limited agricultural export opportunities and job losses in the 1990s, drove continued emigration. The kopu tangata (extended family) remains central to Cook Islander identity, with communities maintaining strong connections through enua associations, churches, and cultural institutions. Religion provided crucial welfare and guidance. Cultural practices including traditional dance, music, tīvaevae (quilting), and language preservation are vital to their heritage. Language preservation faces challenges, with only 10% able to converse in Cook Islands Māori by 2018, though initiatives like punana reo aim to reverse this decline.

6.document_title: Translation and Interpreting in New Zealand: History, Development, and Modern Multilingual Services
6.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of English-Māori translation and interpreting in New Zealand from 1769 to the early 21st century. It begins with Tupaia, a Tahitian chief who interpreted for James Cook's voyage, and covers early missionary translations of Christian texts. A major focus is the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), whose overnight translation by Reverend Henry Williams raised critical questions about accuracy and the meaning of "tino rangatiratanga." The document details how translation services evolved from essential survival tools for early European settlers to formal institutional roles in courts, government, and Parliament. Key figures include Pei Te Hurinui Jones, a prolific translator of English literature into Māori. Modern developments include the 1990 Nga tangata taumata rau translation project, the establishment of full-time Parliamentary interpreters by 1999, the 2013 bilingual Mokomoko Act, and the licensing of interpreters through Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori. 8.document_title: Te Reo Māori: History, Decline, and Revitalisation in New Zealand
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of te reo Māori (the Māori language) from first European contact in 1769 through modern revitalisation efforts. Te reo Māori, a Polynesian language within the Austronesian family, became the official language of New Zealand in 1987. The document details the language's three major dialects and its evolution through early European contact, missionary involvement, and the development of written Māori from the 1820s onward. It chronicles the systematic decline following the Education Ordinance 1847, which mandated English-only education, leading to significant speaker population reduction by the 20th century due to urbanisation, world wars, and assimilationist policies. The revitalisation movement began in the 1970s, including the 1972 te reo petition (30,000 signatures), establishment of Māori Language Week, and the landmark 1984 Māori Language Claim (WAI 11). Key initiatives include kōhanga reo (language immersion centres) established in 1982, kura kaupapa (immersion schools), wharekura (secondary schools), and Te Ataarangi adult learning programmes. The Māori Language Act 1987 established Māori as an official language and created Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori. Broadcasting played a crucial role through Te Upoko o Te Ika radio station (1987), Te Māngai Pāho funding agency (1993), and Māori Television (2004). As of 2018, approximately 21% of Māori and 4% of the total population speak the language.

12.document_title: Te Ao Mārama: Traditional Māori Worldview, Cosmology, and Spiritual Concepts
12.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the traditional Māori worldview and understanding of nature (Te Ao Mārama), presenting a holistic indigenous philosophy centered on interconnectedness and spiritual principles. It explains how Māori people viewed all elements of nature—birds, fish, people, wind, and sun—as an interconnected family linked through genealogies (whakapapa). The creation story describes how earth mother Papatūānuku and sky father Ranginui produced 70 children who became gods of different natural domains. Key concepts include whakapapa (genealogies explaining relationships between all things), Te Kore (a realm of unlimited potential and ultimate reality), and the cycle of light (Te Ao) and darkness (Te Pō) representing birth and death. Three interconnected spiritual concepts are examined: mana (extraordinary power and essence), tapu (sacred restrictions and disciplines), and mauri (life force energy binding all physical things). The document explores tangata whenua (people of the land), where identity is defined through geographical and ancestral connections, and discusses taniwha as spiritual guardians. It emphasizes how orators use speech to guide people from darkness into light, mirroring Tāne's separation of earth and sky, and highlights the practical and spiritual functions of oral traditions in transmitting knowledge while maintaining respect toward other species.

The text explores New Zealand's distinctive political identity shaped by pioneering achievements such as women's suffrage (1893), welfare system development, and progressive social policies including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986) and civil unions (2005). It analyzes political socialization through family, education, media, and personal experiences, while examining how cultural diversity, Māori perspectives, and the Treaty of Waitangi influence contemporary values. The document discusses the nation's shift toward independence and non-alignment since the 1980s, environmental concerns, and movements like the Values Party and anti-nuclearism. Distinctive "Kiwi" characteristics include pragmatism, egalitarianism, tolerance for diverse lifestyles, skepticism toward large powers, and practical problem-solving. New Zealand's political culture reflects social liberalism with subdued patriotism, religious tolerance, secular governance, and self-image as a world leader through idealism and pragmatic innovation. The text contrasts earlier conformist characterizations with contemporary celebration of excellence and diversity.

14.text:
[Page 4] Until the mid 20th century the Māori population was largely rural. Between 1951 and 1971 the proportion of Māori living in cities rose from 20% to 58%. By 2001 Māori were as likely to be living in cities and larger towns as the rest of the population. When Māori and Pākehā began living in closer proximity, the belief that the country had ‘the best race relations in the world’ was tested. A race relations conciliator was first appointed in 1971 to help combat racial discrimination . Pacific Islanders In 2001 about half the 231,800 Pacific Islanders in New Zealand were Samoan . The next largest groups were Cook Island Māori (52,600) and Tongan (40,700). Many more Cook Island Māori, Niueans and Tokelauans live in New Zealand than on their home islands. More than half the Pacific Islanders who live in New Zealand were born there. The population is young and concentrated in the Auckland region. Asians Between 1991 and 2001, the proportion of Asians in New Zealand almost doubled. By 2001, Asians made up 6.6% of the population. Chinese formed the largest group, followed by Indians . Within these two communities there are families that have been in the country for several generations. In 2006 three quarters of New Zealand’s Asians lived in the Auckland region. They have sometimes borne the brunt of anti immigrant sentiment, exploited by some politicians. However, New Zealand society has generally welcomed the newcomers. Languages Most New Zealanders speak only English . But a revival of the Māori language , combined with increasing numbers of immigrants, meant that in the 2000s more than half a million New Zealanders spoke at least one other language. In 2006 Māori was spoken by about 157,000 people. One in four Māori spoke the language, and conscious efforts had been made to keep it alive. The most common language after English and Māori was Samoan, spoken by more than 80,000 people. Other languages with large numbers of speakers included Tongan, Hindi, French and the Chinese dialects of Cantonese and Mandarin.

14.document_title: New Zealand Society: A Comprehensive Overview of Population, Culture, Health, Education, and Modern Life
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's society across multiple dimensions. It covers the nation's diverse population of over 5 million people, including 67% of European descent, significant Māori (565,329), Pacific Islander, and Asian communities. Demographic trends reveal an aging population, declining birth rates, and increasing ethnic diversity concentrated primarily in the North Island, particularly Auckland. The document details family structures, housing trends showing declining home ownership (from 73.8% in 1991 to 67.8% in 2001), and rising single-parent families (31% in 2001). Gender dynamics highlight women's improved economic and social status since the 1980s, alongside New Zealand's progressive LGBTQ+ rights stance, including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986), civil unions (2005), and same-sex marriage (2013). Health outcomes have improved significantly since the 1950s, with life expectancy at 76 years for men and 81 for women (2000), though Māori populations experience lower life expectancy and higher mortality rates. The education system provides free, compulsory state schooling from ages 6-16, with special initiatives like kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa Māori for language preservation. Religion remains important with approximately half the population identifying as Christian, though church attendance is low and religious diversity has increased through immigration. The document traces cultural evolution including the transformation of cuisine from British traditions to cosmopolitan cooking, beverage consumption shifts from beer to wine and coffee, and relaxed dress codes reflecting global influences. Throughout, it highlights both multicultural achievements and persistent socioeconomic disparities faced by Māori communities.

15.text:
[Page 1] Tribal organisation By Rāwiri Taonui What are iwi and hapū? The iwi (tribe) is the largest of the groups that form Māori society. Each iwi is made up of various hapū (clans or descent groups), which might have up to several hundred members. Traditionally, the main purposes of a hapū were to defend land, and to provide support for its members. How iwi and hapū formed Some tribal groups formed from links to the waka (canoe) on which their founding ancestor arrived in New Zealand from Hawaiki. For example, the Waikato tribes trace their descent from the Tainui waka. Others developed when the pressure on resources such as land and food became so great that some members had to move away and establish themselves elsewhere. War, migration and family infighting also caused new iwi or hapū to emerge. Iwi and hapū are often named after an ancestor. For example, Ngāpuhi means ‘the people of Puhi ’ and Te Uri o Rātā means ‘the descendants of Rātā’. Sometimes tribal names came from an important event that involved their ancestor, such as a battle. Whānau family Each hapū is made up of whānau (extended families). Whānau included much respected elders, adults, children and grandchildren. Everyone helped each other, working for the group and caring for each other’s children and the elderly. Social groups Each hapū was made up of different ranking members, headed by chiefs called ariki and rangatira . First born females also had high status. Experts in areas such as history and tradition, carving and healing were called tohunga . There were commoners and sometimes captives or slaves in each hapū . Changes after European contact After New Zealand became a British colony, the way that iwi and hapū functioned began to change. When the government bought or confiscated Māori land in the 19th century, tribes were dispersed. From the mid 20th century, when many younger people moved to the cities for greater work opportunities, tribal power was diminished. From the late 20th century, however, tribal organisations have worked to reconnect people with their tribal origins.

17.text:
[Page 1] The significance of iwi and hapū Iwi The largest political grouping in pre European Māori society was the iwi (tribe). This usually consisted of several related hapū (clans or descent groups). The hapū of an iwi might sometimes fight each other, but would unite to defend tribal territory against other tribes. Iwi tūturu (the homeland tribe) or tino iwi (the central tribe) were groups living in a long held location. They would take their name from a founding ancestor. Iwi nui or iwi whānui (the greater tribe) were groups tracing descent from the founding ancestor of the iwi tūturu. They were often widespread and lived alongside people from other iwi .

18.document_title: Regional Cultural and Creative Life in New Zealand: From the 19th Century to the 2000s
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of regional cultural and creative life in New Zealand from the 19th century through the 2000s. It examines how Māori communities maintained distinct cultural practices including waiata singing, weaving, and carving styles that varied by iwi and region, while European settlements established cultural institutions such as choral societies, museums, and libraries. Dunedin emerged as the most vibrant cultural center due to Scottish settlers and gold wealth, producing notable figures like Thomas Morland Hocken and William Mathew Hodgkins. Other regions developed distinctive cultural scenes: Rotorua fostered Māori culture and early film; Christchurch became a literary hub with the Caxton Press; Wellington attracted writers and developed post-WWII coffee house culture; Auckland became a fashion capital and avant-garde center. The document highlights literary revolutions in the 1930s with publications like Phoenix and Tomorrow, and traces the emergence of distinctive musical genres from the late 1970s onward, including punk in Auckland, the Dunedin sound indie-pop, hip hop in South Auckland, and heavy metal in Waikato. Major cultural events and festivals are examined, including WOMAD in New Plymouth, Art Deco Weekend in Napier, and Polyfest in Auckland. Provincial artistic clusters in Nelson, Whanganui, Taranaki, and Dunedin developed distinct artistic traditions, with Wellington's thriving arts scene and film industry presence highlighted as significant cultural contributions.

19.text:
[Page 1] Linking the people to the land Many Māori traditions tell of the Polynesian settlers from Hawaiki, who reached the coast in canoes about 700 years ago. But there are also myths and legends of earlier beings, such as the first human to be created. Through these stories, tribes can trace a long relationship with the land, and with the different regions they live in. Hineahuone In tradition, Ranginui (the sky father) and Papatūānuku (the earth mother) were the parents of Tāne. Tāne made the first woman from the soil, naming her Hineahuone. One story says ‘the arms, the body, the limbs, the thighs, these all took shape and the skeleton was complete’. With Tāne she had a daughter, Hinetītama, later known as Hine nui te pō, who is seen in the dawn and in the setting sun. It is said that all human beings are descended from these ancestors. Māui The trickster demigod Māui is said to have dragged the North Island from the ocean, using the jawbone of his grandmother as a hook. The Māori name for the island is Te Ika a Māui (Māui’s fish). The many other stories about Māui tell of the theft of fire, the capture of the sun and the pursuit of immortality. Ancestors from the natural world Māori people believed that they were related to the natural world the earth, the birds, the trees. The Ngāi Tūhoe tribe believe that their ancestor was Hine pūkohu rangi, the maiden of the mist that swirled around the Urewera mountains. Patupaiarehe and tūrehu There are many accounts of mysterious people who were already in New Zealand when Polynesian voyagers arrived by canoe. It is said that they lived high in the mountains, and could be heard calling to each other. Two of these groups were known as the patupaiarehe and the tūrehu. Kupe In many traditions, Kupe was the first Polynesian to discover New Zealand. He chased a great octopus across the ocean in his canoe, and finally killed it at Cook Strait. Kupe explored the country and named many places, such as Pari Whero (Red Rocks), on the Wellington coast. Toitehuatahi In some traditions the ancestor Toitehuatahi arrived from Hawaiki, and in others he was born in New Zealand. Tribes are proud to claim they are descended from Toi, and the Ngāti Awa people say his village overlooked the Bay of Plenty, near present day Whakatāne.

19.document_title: Māori Origins, Ancestors, and Tribal Narratives: Creation Mythology, Kupe, Toi, and the Connection Between People and Land
19.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori tribal traditions, creation mythology, and ancestral narratives that form the foundation of Māori cultural identity and connection to Aotearoa New Zealand. It presents a genealogical framework beginning with creation stories featuring Hineahuone, the first human created from earth by Tāne, and the demigod Māui who legendarily fished up the North Island. The text examines pre-canoe narratives of mysterious beings like patupaiarehe and tūrehu, and early explorers and ancestors including Kupe and Toitehuatahi (Toi). Central to the narratives is Kupe, credited as the first Polynesian discoverer of New Zealand, whose journey pursued a giant octopus and resulted in naming locations across the islands, with his wife Kuramārōtini naming Aotearoa ('long white cloud'). The document also emphasizes Toi's significance as an early ancestor recognized as tangata whenua (people of the land), with strong associations to the Whakatāne district and influence among Ngāti Awa, Mataatua, and Ngāi Tūhoe peoples. These interconnected narratives illustrate an organic worldview where earth, sea, and sky possess mana and human qualities, enabling Māori to identify with natural elements. The traditions establish deep connections between Māori tribes and the land, forming the basis for tribal identity, tenure, ancestral authority, and the spiritual relationship between Māori people and their environment across generations.

20.text:
[Page 1] Early settlement The ancestors of Māori arrived on canoes from Pacific islands before 1300 CE. Settling first on the coast, they hunted seals and moas. They also began to grow food, and some moved to the forests. They lived in small tribal groups, with a rich culture of spoken stories, and strong traditions of warfare. Their ancestors, and the gods of the natural world, were very important. Europeans arrive The arrival of Europeans from the early 1800s had a major effect on these early communities. Among the newcomers were missionaries, and many Māori became Christians. They learnt to read and write and began trading, especially in pigs and potatoes. The Treaty of Waitangi signed in 1840 established British law and government, but it could not prevent warfare in the 1840s and 1860s as Māori defended their lands and local authority. After the wars Māori lost land through confiscation and sale, mostly to British settlers. Revival In the first half of the 20th century important leaders such as Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi worked to make life better for Māori and to revive the culture. There was a new interest in the language, and in arts such as carving and weaving. After the Second World War many Māori moved to the cities in search of jobs. In the 1970s and 1980s groups protested about their rights to land, and helped promote the language and culture. Important events were a march down the North Island to Parliament in 1975, the creation of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975 to look at claimed breaches of the Treaty, and the occupation of Bastion Point in Auckland by protesters in 1977 78. Māori today In 2019 there were nearly 800,000 Māori people, with most living in cities. There were kōhanga reo (preschool language nests) and schools using the Māori language, two Māori television channels and 21 radio stations, 29 members of Parliament who identified as Māori, and many creative projects in film, music and art. 20.document_title: Māori: History, Culture, and Contemporary Society in New Zealand
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

21.document_title: Waka: Māori and Moriori Canoes, Cultural Heritage, and Maritime Traditions
21.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores waka (canoes), essential vessels in Māori and Moriori culture and maritime history. It traces waka from their Polynesian origins as double-hulled voyaging canoes that carried the first settlers to Aotearoa (New Zealand) over a month-long journey, to their evolution into specialized single-hulled vessels adapted to New Zealand's abundant large forests. The text describes major waka types including waka taua (war canoes up to 30 metres, holding 100 people), waka tētē (fishing and trading canoes), waka tīwai (river canoes), waka tangata (educational canoes), and mōkihi (rafts), with regional variations such as East Coast and South Island mōkihi rafts, and Moriori waka from the Chatham Islands including waka pūhara, waka rimu, waka pahī, and waka rā. The document details construction methods, including tree selection, carving, and ceremonial practices, and explains how waka design changed as Māori adapted to New Zealand's resources and geography. It covers essential waka equipment including paddles (hoe), sails (rā), poling poles (toko), anchors (punga), and bailers, with detailed descriptions of bailing systems such as puna wai or tāinga ā wai designated areas and intricately carved bailers known as tatā, tīheru, and tā wai. An New Zealand academic says there is a lack of understanding on the details of Aotearoa's relationship with the Cook Islands. Earlier this year, New Zealand extended its funding pause to its realm country "reluctantly", with the total now nearly $30 million over two years. The disagreement between the two governments stem from several agreements that the Cook Islands signed with China at the beginning of the year. The New Zealand government believed it was not adequately consulted over the agreements, which Wellington sees as a requirement under the free association agreement. Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown has pushed back at this, saying the requirement of consultation is mutual, adding New Zealand would not speak to his government prior to signing international deals. The Cook Islands celebrated 60 years of self governance this year. Brown said the nation had evolved, having a paternal relationship with New Zealand to now one of friendship. However, honorary senior lecturer academic researcher at the University of Auckland John McCaffery said it is a sad situation and "neither party really understands the constitutional basis for the relationship". He said more recent agreements, like the 2001 Joint Centenary Declaration signed between New Zealand Prime Minister Helen Clark and Terepai Maoate, are a "superficial issue". "The real issue lies in what is the relationship under the provisions of the realm of New Zealand," McCaffery said. "The realm provisions have remained the same since it was put in place in 1917, when the Cook Islands and Niue were brought into a relationship with New Zealand, not as dependent territories, but actually as an integrated part of the realm of New Zealand, over which the British monarch has absolute authority, which is delegated to the New Zealand Governor General. "I'm not saying that I like it or anybody else likes it but that is the historical situation." The 1917 letters patent established the office of the Governor General and extended its powers to the Cook Islands and Niue. He said it means the New Zealand government has the power to advise the Crown to withdraw the warrant of the current government of the Cook Islands effectively toppling Brown. [Page 1] Mark Brown rejects talk of 'strategic shift' in Cook Islands New Zealand relationship ByCaleb Fotheringham RNZ Pacific Journalist 2025 08 06 08:00:05+12:00 The Cook Islands has no intention of leaving its special relationship with New Zealand, Prime Minister Mark Brown says. The Cook Islands marked 60 years of self governance in free association with New Zealand on 4 August. https://www.rnz.co.nz/international/programmes/datelinepacific/ audio/2018998661/cook islands relationship with nz will remain pm mar k brown "The value of our relationship with New Zealand cannot be overstated," Brown said at the national auditorium in Rarotonga on Monday. His remarks were met with a round of applause. "I would like to emphasise that there is not now, nor has there ever been, a strategic shift by the Cook Islands government or our peoples to reject the value and responsibilities of our relationship of free association with New Zealand." The celebration was filled with dancing, singing, food and a 45 minute speech by Brown on where the nation has come from and where it's going. "Every island holds a piece of our future, let us stand with conviction on the global stage. Our people span oceans. Our voice carries across borders. And our contribution continues to grow," Brown said. Notably absent from the four Pacific leaders attending was New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who is in Papua New Guinea. Foreign Minister Winston Peters was also absent. Brown said like any relationship, there will be moments that needed reflection. "There are times when we must pause and consider whether the conventions and evolved understandings between our freely associated states remain aligned, we find ourselves in such a moment. "I see our relationship as one grounded in enduring kinship, like members of a family who continue to care deeply for one another, even as each has grown and charted their own path." Brown called the current issues a bump in the road. He said they had been through far worse, like natural disasters and the Covid 19 pandemic. "[The relationship] is too well entrenched and too strong, like steel, that nothing will break it, it is too strong that even disagreeing governments will not break it." Representing New Zealand was Governor General Dame Cindy Kiro, who also talked of the long standing relationship, stemming back hundreds of years to voyaging ancestors. "That bond of deep friendship between our two peoples, that will transcend all else as we continue to face the challenges, and celebrate the joys of the future, together." After the official ceremony, there was a big kai kai. Those attending shared their thoughts on what they wanted for the future of their country. "To see our future generations grow up in our own paradise instead of them going overseas," one woman said. Another said she wanted the Cook Islands to remain a Christian nation and to keep their culture strong. One nurse said medical was always on the go and wanted more investment, "the resources we have are very limited, so I want to see a bigger improvement within our medical side of things". A dentist wanted the Cook Islands to be "a modern nation" and "to be a leader in economic wealth." Another man wanted to remain in free association with New Zealand but wanted the country "to make its own decisions and stand on its own two feet". A primary school principal said he wanted more young people to learn Cook Islands Māori. "This is our identity, our language." He also wanted the country to be more independent economically. "I think we as a nation need to look at how we can support other countries… I don't like that we're still asking for money from New Zealand, from Australia, at some point in the future I would like us as a nation to help other nations." New Zealand paused close to $20 million in development funding in June, citing a lack of consultation on agreements signed between the Cook Islands and China earlier in the year. China's ambassador to New Zealand, Wang Xiaolong was attending the event. RNZ Pacific approached him, but the ambassador said he was unable to comment because he had to leave the event. Related

[Page 1] South Auckland local boards help sustain traditional arts and culture this Cook Islands Language Week 2024 08 12 12:51:59+12:00 By Mary Afemata, Local Democracy Reporter It's another busy day at the Māngere Town Centre. But one particular corner of this small bustling mall is bursting with colour and laughter as elderly women, adorned with beautiful flowery 'ei katu garlands, sew and weave materials in much the same way that their ancestors would have. Among the vibrant group is tivaevae expert and Cook Islands heritage artist Tukua Turia who knows too well the significance of traditional quilt making and stresses the importance of preserving and passing on the knowledge of creating it. "Treasure them ... the good work," she says of the cultural craftsmanship that's laid out around her. An 'ei katu is an arrangement of flowers worn on or around your head like a crown. The tivaevae is another treasured item in the Cook Islands culture, usually a quilt, that is stitched and hand sewn, by older women within the family. And thanks to the Ōtara Papatoetoe and Māngere Ōtāhuhu Local Board, the wider community has been able to learn how to make their own tivaevae and 'ei katu. "It's important ... that's our hope, to learn and not to forget what our grandmothers, our grand aunties taught us, right? So we picked it up," says Turia. Turia is self taught and has been sewing and designing since her twenties. Her work has been commissioned for Te Papa and Auckland Museum, and in the 2019 New Year's Honours she was made a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit for her services to Cook Islands art and culture. "This one here, we do it, you know, all week [for] Cook Islands language, " she says of the free sessions. Turia also runs twice weekly workshops as part of her Creative Polynesian Arts Mamas group. "We keep on doing the same thing, you know but different patterns. We don't do the same pattern. I don't allow them to copy the pattern because you've got to do free hands then you get more," says Turia of her regular classes. Turia says the art of tivaevae is important for its cultural knowledge to be passed on. "To me, it's something that I will never, you know ... forget to pass on to my kids and take them ... that's why I want to do it. It's important for our young generations ... [and] that's what Cook Islands people like to do. It's important. That's our culture." She says the older the tivaevae, the more culturally important it is especially because the creators of these the patterns may have passed. "They're gone. The patrons, the people, the ladies ... the ones who made it like grandmothers. They have passed on. That's why you have to look after them, treasure Ōtara Papatoetoe Local Board chair Apulu Reece Autagavaia says the workshops are part of the board's commitment to sustain Cook Islands culture. "Language is a central part of our identities as people of the Pacific diaspora. Of course, some are more fluent than others but we are all on a journey. Language weeks are one of the ways our Pacific communities can highlight the importance of the language and culture but also to share with others. So, it's not just about the languages, but the customs and values behind our cultural identities. It covers the nation's diverse population of over 5 million people, including 67% of European descent, significant Māori (565,329), Pacific Islander, and Asian communities. Demographic trends reveal an aging population, declining birth rates, and increasing ethnic diversity concentrated primarily in the North Island, particularly Auckland. The document details family structures, housing trends showing declining home ownership (from 73.8% in 1991 to 67.8% in 2001), and rising single-parent families (31% in 2001). Gender dynamics highlight women's improved economic and social status since the 1980s, alongside New Zealand's progressive LGBTQ+ rights stance, including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986), civil unions (2005), and same-sex marriage (2013). Health outcomes have improved significantly since the 1950s, with life expectancy at 76 years for men and 81 for women (2000), though Māori populations experience lower life expectancy and higher mortality rates. The education system provides free, compulsory state schooling from ages 6-16, with special initiatives like kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa Māori for language preservation. Religion remains important with approximately half the population identifying as Christian, though church attendance is low and religious diversity has increased through immigration. The document traces cultural evolution including the transformation of cuisine from British traditions to cosmopolitan cooking, beverage consumption shifts from beer to wine and coffee, and relaxed dress codes reflecting global influences. Throughout, it highlights both multicultural achievements and persistent socioeconomic disparities faced by Māori communities.

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

chunkHighlights.text:
Early settlement The ancestors of Māori arrived on canoes from Pacific
islands before 1300 CE. Settling first on the coast, they hunted seals and moas. They also began to grow food, and some moved to the forests. They lived in small tribal groups, with a rich culture of spoken stories, and strong traditions of warfare. Their ancestors, and the gods of the natural world, were very important. Europeans arrive The arrival of Europeans from the early 1800s had a major effect on these early communities. Among the newcomers were missionaries, and many Māori became Christians. They learnt to read and write and began trading, especially in pigs and potatoes. The Treaty of Waitangi signed in 1840 established British law and government, but it could not prevent warfare in the 1840s and 1860s as Māori defended their lands and local authority. After the wars Māori lost land through confiscation and sale, mostly to British settlers. Revival In the first half of the 20th century important leaders such as Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi worked to make life better for Māori and to revive the culture. There was a new interest in the language, and in arts such as carving and weaving. After the Second World War many Māori moved to the cities in search of jobs. In the 1970s and 1980s groups protested about their rights to land, and helped promote the language and culture. Important events were a march down the North Island to Parliament in 1975, the creation of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975 to look at claimed breaches of the Treaty, and the occupation of Bastion Point in Auckland by protesters in 1977–78. There were kōhanga reo (preschool language nests) and schools using the Māori language, two Māori television channels and 21 radio stations, 29 members of Parliament who identified as Māori, and many creative projects in film, music and art. 5.fileDescription: A disagreement between New Zealand and Cook Islands governments has escalated over China agreements signed by the Cook Islands at the beginning of 2025. New Zealand paused nearly $30 million in funding over two years, citing inadequate consultation under the free association agreement. University of Auckland academic John McCaffery highlights a fundamental constitutional misunderstanding, explaining that under 1917 letters patent, the Cook Islands remains an integrated part of the New Zealand realm with the Governor-General holding ultimate authority—not an independent nation. McCaffery suggests the Cook Islands should seek amendments to the letters patent rather than clarification on self-governance. New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters emphasizes the relationship is with the Cook Islands people and calls for a referendum if independence is desired. The dispute reflects deeper tensions over the nature of the realm relationship and the limits of Cook Islands autonomy.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history of te reo Māori (the Māori language) from first European contact in 1769 through modern revitalisation efforts. Te reo Māori, a Polynesian language within the Austronesian family, became the official language of New Zealand in 1987. The document details the language's three major dialects and its evolution through early European contact, missionary involvement, and the development of written Māori from the 1820s onward. It chronicles the systematic decline following the Education Ordinance 1847, which mandated English-only education, leading to significant speaker population reduction by the 20th century due to urbanisation, world wars, and assimilationist policies. The revitalisation movement began in the 1970s, including the 1972 te reo petition (30,000 signatures), establishment of Māori Language Week, and the landmark 1984 Māori Language Claim (WAI 11). Key initiatives include kōhanga reo (language immersion centres) established in 1982, kura kaupapa (immersion schools), wharekura (secondary schools), and Te Ataarangi adult learning programmes. The Māori Language Act 1987 established Māori as an official language and created Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori. Broadcasting played a crucial role through Te Upoko o Te Ika radio station (1987), Te Māngai Pāho funding agency (1993), and Māori Television (2004). As of 2018, approximately 21% of Māori and 4% of the total population speak the language.

chunkHighlights.text: Māori is part of the Austronesian language family, which is found through South-East Asia and the Pacific. It is one of a number of Polynesian languages and comes under the Tahitic branch, as do Tahitian, Cook Island Māori and languages of the Tuamotu Archipelago. It is also closely related to the Moriori language of the Chatham Islands.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the migration history and settlement patterns of Cook Islanders in New Zealand from the early 20th century through 2018. Beginning with small numbers of soldiers and students in the 1920s-1930s, migration accelerated significantly after WWII as young people sought better wages and urban opportunities. By 1976, over 12,000 Cook Islanders had settled in New Zealand, eventually reaching 61,000 by 2013 and over 80,000 by 2018—outnumbering those remaining on the islands. Early migrants concentrated in major cities including Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch, working in factory, domestic, canning, and timber mill jobs. Chain migration became prevalent from the 1960s onward as established residents sponsored family members. Economic factors, including limited agricultural export opportunities and job losses in the 1990s, drove continued emigration. The kopu tangata (extended family) remains central to Cook Islander identity, with communities maintaining strong connections through enua associations, churches, and cultural institutions. Religion provided crucial welfare and guidance. Cultural practices including traditional dance, music, tīvaevae (quilting), and language preservation are vital to their heritage. Language preservation faces challenges, with only 10% able to converse in Cook Islands Māori by 2018, though initiatives like punana reo aim to reverse this decline.

chunkHighlights.text: While different islands have different dialects, Rarotongan has emerged as the dominant Cook Islands Māori language. Even this is a candidate for the endangered language list, not only in New Zealand but also in Rarotonga. In the 1960s many older migrants spoke only their own tongue at home, while younger people were increasingly speaking English.

chunkHighlights.text:
By Aui'a Vaimaila Leatinu'u, PMN Gerardine Clifford-Lidstone Pacific
people who marry outside their heritage often choose Māori partners, according to a Ministry for Pacific Peoples (MPP) investigation into this increasingly shared identity among these populations. According to MPP's ongoing Insights Briefing, which aims to deepen the understanding of Māori and Pacific identity, there are around 90,000 people who identify as both Māori and Pacific in Aotearoa. "We also found that when Pacific people marry outside of [their culture], they will marry a Māori first," Gerardine Clifford-Lidstone, the Secretary for Pacific Peoples at MPP, told Khalia Strong on Pacific Mornings. "While we're different, there's also a lot of similarities. What I've found, as I've gone around talking to various iwi leaders, is that…we want these populations to be counted. "There are so many that have said, 'my moko [grandchild] is part Tongan, part Māori, and they speak both Māori and Tongan'. Others say, 'I know someone in my whānau, who's part Cook Island, part Māori, and they want to learn their Cook Island whakapapa' because they've been raised entirely with a Māori worldview." Clifford-Lidstone emphasised the significance of understanding these identities, saying that by 2043, nearly 40 per cent of New Zealand's population will identify as Māori or Pacific, which will impact workforce demographics, cultural experiences, language, and genealogical ties moving forward. "It's been a really fun and insightful process to participate in. The consultation's open for one more week, 9 July. I really encourage people who identify as both Māori and Pacific to participate." Budget cuts The MPP is facing nearly $36 million in funding reductions under Budget 2025, following a previous cut of $26m. Despite this, key policy priorities have been retained, with some new initiatives introduced. For example, the Tauola Business Fund ended and the Tupu Aotearoa employment programme scaled back, while funding for the Pacific Business Trust and Pacific Business Village continues. Despite a tighter budget, Clifford-Lidstone says major initiatives continue, including the Pacific Languages Strategy, Toloa STEM scholarships, and
Pacific Media
Innovation funding. "Then we've got our housing

initiatives. So, the building of affordable homes, a programme as part of
that called Our Whare Our Fale, which is looking at 300 homes in Porirua. Then the Financial Capability Programme. You may have seen in Budget 2025 some new money for Pacific Wardens," she says. "These really wonderful mātua and volunteers from our community who support the work of a range of agencies, particularly police, engaging with the community and ensuring that we are in a safe environment. We've still got a lot of work underway there on top of our policy programme." On the legacy Dawn Raids programme, she says the funding will remain until the 2026 to 2027 period, with the Vaka of Stories project helping to capture community narratives. Clifford-Lidstone adds that they have two years to complete specific deliverables, some of which have already been completed. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a4pVL3guMu4&em beds_referring_euri=https%3A%2F%2Fpmn.co.nz%2F&source_ve_path= MjM4NTE Census data cancellation She acknowledges the concerns around the planned cancellation of the nationwide Census survey, emphasising the importance of evidence-based data for delivering targeted services. Clifford-Lidstone says the Pacific community's pace of growth and change is rapid. "Our data and insights team have a formal agreement with Statistics New Zealand to work together on census planning and data standards. So, we're going to be working really closely with them to keep an eye on that particular issue. "We do want our communities to be accurately reflected and to be participating. That participation will change a little bit given that it's on admin data, we need the quality of that admin data to be good. So, that's a role that we
will be playing." -This article was first published by PMN. Related
